Then, when the emir seeing no help coming from the people of Baghdad,
took refuge with the Romans.
And he sent an envoy to King Basil,
and humbled himself before him and sought help from him.
He, then, sent him fifty thousand horsemen and foot soldiers.
And while the army of the Romans was encamped on the river Orontes,
which is the Asi,
which is beside Antioch,
the armies of the Egyptians hastened and went and crossed the river,
and encountered the Romans and defeated them,
and returned and encamped against Aleppo.
Lulu, then, used a ruse,
and bribed Manjutakin with much gold.
And he left it and returned to Damascus,
and wrote to al-Aziz that the armies that were with him were perishing from hunger,
and on this account I have come to Damascus,
so that when they have regained strength, we may return.
Al-Aziz, however, became enraged,
especially since it was reported {OCR?}
that he had not come to Damascus for this reason,
but in order to indulge in luxury,
because he was a youth without scars as yet.
Therefore he dismissed him,
and appointed in his place as commander of the army a certain Rudbari {OCR?},
and sent him again against Aleppo.
And he began to transport grain for the armies from Alexandria by sea,
and stored two hundred thousand qafizes of wheat and barley in the district of Apamea.
And they used to go twenty-five parasangs from Aleppo to there,
and take provisions for their horses.
And they sat besieging Aleppo for thirteen
months,
and built for themselves baths, inns, and shops.
And famine grew very severe inside the city.
It is said
that Lulu would buy a qafiz for three dinars,
and sell it for one dinar to the citizens of the city,
so that they would not be too hard pressed.
And he again used a ruse, and sent once more an envoy to King Basil, and said to him:
"If you do not overtake him with a large army,
behold, these men will gain control over Aleppo,
and immediately you must not suppose that Antioch will remain yours."
And on this account Basil was stirred up and gathered an army,
and marched three hundred parasangs in sixteen days with thirty thousand Romans.
And he arrived and struck the spring-pastures of the horses of the Egyptians,
which were grazing in the meadows,
because it was spring.
Lulu, however, sent a message to the Rudbarian and said to him:
"The neighborhood in which we share with one another calls me to pity towards you and towards your armies.
Be on your guard from now on;"
